anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.text:
**(1) First message**

The gather draft's claims are supported only by the draft, because I made no tool calls in this session. It says the reports page renders a table with no export action, that the table's column definitions and the existing CSV serializer in `src/export/csv.ts` already support export, and that paging supports the 10k-row target. The design rests on those claims, and I'm treating them as supported by the draft rather than verified against code.

One premise is unverified. The 10k-row row needs a way to prove "under 60s": a 10k-row report fixture or dataset and a timing run. The draft names neither. The lookup would be a search of the test fixtures and seed data for a large report, plus a timed export against it. I haven't done that lookup, so the 60s claim goes into Open Questions instead of blocking the design.

The framing holds. Its basis is the draft's report that the reports page has no export action and the `Pattern:` line saying `src/export/csv.ts` already reuses the table's column definitions. The ask adds an action on top of an existing serializer and existing column source. It is not a second parallel path.

The ticket groups its rows by repo. The `acme/widgets` group matches this repo (overrides `repo: acme/widgets`), so its three rows are this brainstorm's contract. The `phase 2` heading matches no repo, so the emailed-export row needs a call. Where does the `phase 2` row belong?
A) this repo
B) elsewhere: phase 2
C) repair the ticket - /skill:shape-ticket acme/widgets#77
Recommendation: C - "phase 2" reads as a delivery stage rather than a repo, so the ticket should say where that row lives instead of the spec guessing.

---

**(2) Approaches message**

First, the missing dependency. Proving "a 10k-row export completes in under 60s" requires a 10k-row report fixture and a timed run. The draft names neither, so the lookup is a fixture/seed search plus a timed export, and it is not yet done. The row stays in-scope, and whether such a fixture exists goes into Open Questions. Each approach below has to say how it would be timed.

From your answers, the button sits beside the report title. "Every column shown in the table" is read as the visible table columns, in table order, and that reading becomes a Design clause. The emailed-export row waits on the `phase 2` answer. None of the approaches below depends on it, except where noted in the third.

What separates the approaches is where the full row set is gathered and serialized: in the browser, on the server, or in a background job.

**Recommended: reuse the existing serializer from the page.** The Export CSV button next to the report title walks the reports table's existing paging to collect all rows. It passes them, with the table's visible column definitions in table order, to the CSV serializer in `src/export/csv.ts`, then triggers a download. This is the reuse-only option, since it adds no new construct beyond the button and its handler. Its risk is the 10k-row case: browser memory, and page round-trips that each add latency. The draft's statement that paging supports the target is the evidence that this fits inside 60s. A timed test against a 10k-row fixture would confirm it.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title; click handler that pages through the report data and calls the existing serializer with the visible column definitions; test timing a 10k-row export; test asserting exported columns match visible table columns in order
Pattern: follows `src/export/csv.ts`, which already reuses the table's column definitions, so the export and the table share one column source.

**Server-side streaming export.** A new export endpoint pages through the report on the server and streams CSV through the same serializer and column definitions. The button just requests it. This separates export speed and memory from the client, and it scales past 10k rows. The cost is a new endpoint and a second place that must know which columns are "visible." Column visibility is currently a table concern, so the client would have to send the visible column list or the server would duplicate that logic.
Removes: none
Adds: export endpoint; server-side paging loop; request parameter carrying the visible column list; button wiring to the endpoint; endpoint timing test at 10k rows; column-order test
Pattern: reuses `src/export/csv.ts` but moves the column-visibility decision across a boundary it doesn't own today.

**Background export job (drops the assumption that the export is an immediate download).** The button enqueues a job that builds the CSV, and the user collects a download link when it's ready. This is the natural home for the `phase 2` emailing row if you answer A. It also blurs the 60s row into "job finishes within 60s" instead of "download completes." Unless the emailing row lands in this repo, it adds a job runner, job state, and a notification path that nothing in this ticket needs.
Removes: none
Adds: export job type; job status storage; link/notification surface; button wiring; job-duration test at 10k rows
Pattern: introduces a new asynchronous path beside the synchronous serializer in `src/export/csv.ts`. That is justified only by a requirement this repo doesn't yet own.

I'd go with the first approach. It meets all three `acme/widgets` rows with the parts that already exist. The recommendation flips to the server-side endpoint if a timed 10k-row run in the browser misses 60s or exhausts memory. It flips to the background job if the `phase 2` row turns out to belong to this repo.
